title: Matthew 16:5–12
context: Crossing the lake, the disciples fret about forgotten bread while Jesus warns them of the yeast of the Pharisees and Sadducees. He recalls the feedings, exposes their little faith, and clarifies that the danger is false teaching, not empty baskets.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Arminian and Reformed writers of the past on crossing the lake, in their own words.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees - That is, of their false doctrine: this is elegantly so called; for it spreads in the soul, or the Church, as leaven does in meal. They reasoned among themselves - What must we do then for bread, since we have taken no bread with us?
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on Matt 16:5–12)

reformed.quote: Here Christ takes occasion from the circumstance that had just occurred to exhort his disciples to beware of every abuse that makes an inroad on sincere piety. The Pharisees had come a little before; the Sadducees joined them; and apart from them stood Herod, a very wicked man, and an opponent and corrupter of sound doctrine.
reformed.source: Commentary on a Harmony of the Evangelists (on Matt 16:5–12)

verses.text: The disciples came to the other side and had forgotten to take bread.
verses.arminianNotes:
A small forgetfulness opens the next lesson. The disciples arrive empty-handed, preoccupied with provision they can see.

Arminian pastoral reading notices ordinary human anxiety under grace: followers of Jesus still misplace attention. The Lord will not scold hunger; He will redirect trust.
verses.reformedNotes:
Matthew’s detail is deliberate: forgotten bread becomes the stage for a warning about doctrine.

Reformed preaching often marks providence in small scenes—the Lord uses even the disciples’ lapse to teach. Need becomes the classroom where Christ corrects faith.

verses.text: Jesus said to them, “Take heed and beware of the yeast of the Pharisees and Sadducees.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“Take heed and beware” is a living command. Leaven works quietly; so does corrupting teaching. Jesus protects His friends by naming the danger.

Arminians hear enabling grace in the warning itself: God does not leave disciples to drift. He calls for vigilant, responsible discernment that grace makes possible.
verses.reformedNotes:
Christ shepherds his disciples by warning them. Leaven is small, pervasive, and transforming—an apt image for teaching that spreads through a community.

The Lord who feeds multitudes also guards His church’s mind. Truth and error are not equal options; Jesus commands separation from soul-spoiling doctrine.

verses.text: They reasoned among themselves, saying, “We brought no bread.”
verses.arminianNotes:
They hear “yeast” and think lunch. Spiritual metaphor collapses into logistics. The miss is almost comic—and deeply human.

Even sincere disciples can resist clarity by staying in the safer worry. Grace keeps addressing them anyway.
verses.reformedNotes:
Mishearing Jesus is not rare among His own. Their private conference fixes on scarcity rather than the Teacher’s intent.

The Reformed note is patience and realism: without illumination, even recent miracles fade from practical memory. Christ must explain Himself again.

verses.text: Jesus, perceiving it, said, “Why do you reason among yourselves, you of little faith, because you have brought no bread?
verses.arminianNotes:
He knows their talk and names the root: little faith, not merely empty packs. Faith here is trust that should already have learned from His generosity.

Arminians treat “little faith” as a true but incomplete trust—grace has begun, yet the heart still shrinks. The rebuke invites growth, not despair.
verses.reformedNotes:
Omniscient kindness: Jesus answers the conversation they never voiced to Him. “Little faith” diagnoses unbelief’s scale, not its absence.

Christ preserves and corrects weak disciples. Their faith is His gift under repair, not a self-made strength that failed a test.

verses.text: Don’t you yet perceive or remember the five loaves for the five thousand, and how many baskets you took up,
verses.arminianNotes:
Memory is a servant of faith. Jesus points them back to baskets already counted—evidence they handled with their own hands.

God has given enough light in experience and Word for a trusting response. Forgetting mercy is a moral failure grace still seeks to heal.
verses.reformedNotes:
“Yet” marks delayed perception despite privilege. The feedings were not mere wonders; they were tutorials in the Lord’s sufficiency.

Remembrance is commanded because God has acted. Faith feeds on God’s deeds; unbelief edits the past until anxiety feels reasonable.

verses.text: or the seven loaves for the four thousand, and how many baskets you took up?
verses.arminianNotes:
A second feeding doubles the witness. Abundance repeated should silence panic about bread.

Christ is a generous Lord. Arminians press the invitation to keep trusting the One who has already provided.
verses.reformedNotes:
Two banquets, two tallies of leftovers—Matthew’s Jesus insists the pattern is clear.

Sovereignty here is practical: the very Lord who multiplied loaves rules their present lack. Anxiety about bread insults a proven Provider.

verses.text: How is it that you don’t perceive that I didn’t speak to you concerning bread? But beware of the yeast of the Pharisees and Sadducees.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jesus restates the warning without softening it. The issue is teaching that ferments unbelief and hypocrisy, not bakery yeast.

Hearers remain responsible to understand and obey. Grace clarifies; disciples must not hide in confusion when Christ speaks plainly.
verses.reformedNotes:
Failure to understand is exposed, then healed by repetition. Christ will not let the metaphor stay muddled.

The Shepherd teaches until the point lands. Doctrine matters because false leaven ruins the loaf of the church’s faith.

verses.text: Then they understood that he didn’t tell them to beware of the yeast of bread, but of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees.
verses.arminianNotes:
Understanding finally dawns. The danger is doctrinal and spiritual—teachings that puff pride, demand signs, and miss the Messiah.

Classical Arminians celebrate this as grace-enabled insight that still involves learning. God opens minds; disciples truly come to see.
verses.reformedNotes:
Matthew closes the scene with illumination granted. What they could not grasp, they now grasp because Jesus persisted.

Christ not only warns; He gives understanding. The church is kept from deadly teaching by the Lord’s effective instruction.
verses.keyContrast: Both prize Christ’s warning and the disciples’ eventual clarity. Arminians typically describe understanding as grace-enabled perception disciples must embrace; Reformed readers commonly stress Christ’s effective teaching that secures true understanding in His own.
